title: Open the account after a loss?
hook: Would a market drop change when you choose to look at your portfolio?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Separate attention to an outcome from the investment outcome itself.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Separate attention to an outcome from the investment outcome itself.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy account starts at €100 and loses 10%. If the owner does not open the account and makes no trades, what is its value? Toy inputs A=[100, -10, 0]; B=[100, 10, 1].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[90, 0, -10], [110.00000000000001, 1, 10]]. Labels: Ending value €, Checks, Return %.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: Checking behavior and portfolio performance are separate variables. In this no-trading model, failing to look does not undo the return. The observed tendency to avoid bad news would require behavioral evidence beyond the balance calculation.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Starting value €=100, Return %=10, Account checks=1. What is Ending value €? Answer: 110.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Starting value €=100, Return %=10, Account checks=1. What is Ending value €?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 110. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Investors look up their portfolios less after market declines, the "ostrich effect" (Karlsson, Loewenstein & Seppi, 2009).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Separate attention to an outcome from the investment outcome itself.
